arguments.audience: First-year calculus learners meeting limits for the first time
arguments.central_takeaway: A limit is a claim about values arbitrarily near a target, supported by a controllable input-output neighborhood relationship.
arguments.closing_resolution: The neighborhood relationship makes approach precise while leaving the value at the target logically separate.
arguments.learning_objective: Explain a finite limit using neighborhoods and distinguish approach behavior from the function value at the target.
arguments.opening_question: How can a function approach one value without reaching it?

body: Watch the inputs move toward the target while the outputs settle near one value.
slides.narrative_job: Create the need for a language of controlled approach.
slides.primary_claim: Nearness, not arrival, is the phenomenon we need to describe.
slides.speaker_notes: Invite learners to describe what remains stable during approach.
slides.title: A function can approach a value it never reaches

bullets: The output band is centered on the proposed limit.
The input band is centered on the target.
Every permitted input must land inside the output band.
slides.narrative_job: Replace informal motion language with a controllable relationship.
slides.primary_claim: A chosen output tolerance determines how close inputs must be.
slides.speaker_notes: Name every symbol before reading the implication aloud.
slides.title: Two linked neighborhoods make approach measurable

slides.narrative_job: Demonstrate the control relationship without skipping algebra.
slides.primary_claim: For f(x)=2x+1 near x=3, choosing delta=epsilon/2 is sufficient.
slides.speaker_notes: Keep the implication direction explicit at each step.
slides.title: For a line, the needed input band follows directly

body: You can now test a proposed limit by connecting any requested output tolerance to a sufficient input tolerance.
slides.narrative_job: Resolve the opening question and state the reusable understanding.
slides.primary_claim: Controlled neighborhoods explain approach even when f(a) differs or is absent.
slides.speaker_notes: Return to the opening example and separate the hole from the nearby trend.
slides.title: The limit records stable local behavior, not a point value
